To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the presence of >2 TIL cells per HPF, the lack of a dirty necrosis, right-sided location and age <50, any mucinous component, and a Crohn-like inflammatory reaction are the most significant predictors of microsatellite instabilty.

12% of CRCs are MSI-H; the presence of dirty necrosis and the absence of a Crohn's-like reaction are the most powerful predictors of microsatellite stability; and a simple logistic regression model can accurately predict the likelihood of MSI-H based on the presence of these and other pathologic features.

the presence of >2 tumor-inflitrating lymphocyte cells (TIL) per high powered field, the lack dirty necrosis, and the presence of a crohn-like reaction, a right sided location and any mucinous differentiation are independent predictors of high microsatellite instability.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of pathologic predictors of microsatellite instable colorectal cancers (MSI-H).
the development of a model to predict microsatellite unstable colorectal cancers (MSI-H CRCs) based on a population-based study of 1649 tumors from patients of all age groups.
a better understanding of the molecular and genetic events that lead to the development of colorectal cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MSI probability scores of 1 or greater (approximately 57% of CRCs) should be considered for further MSI testing.

the use of the MSI probability score is not recommended for the routine clinical setting, but that it may have a role in the research setting, particularly when the cost and availability of microsatellite analysis are limiting.
MSI-H is a rare, but not uncommon, event in CRCs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the combination of a Crohn’s like lymphocytic infiltrate, a low number of TILs, and a right-sided tumor is a strong predictor of MSI-H.

MSI-H CRCs are characterized by the lack of dirty (diffuse) necrosis, a Crohn-like lymphoid reaction, and a well or poorly differentiated mucinous or focally-mucinous histology, and are associated with age <50 and right-sided location.

MSI-H tumors are more likely to be located on the right colon, to have a Crohn-like inflammatory reaction, to be well or poorly differentiated, to be focally mucinous or mucinous, to be associated with an increased number of tumor-infiltrating T cells, and to occur in patients younger than 50.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the pathologist can use a combination of clinical and histologic features to identify a subset of tumors that are highly unlikely to have microsatellite instability.
a combination of clinical factors, such as age, and histologic features, such as dirty necrosis, can be used to predict MSI-H in a CRC.
pathologists should consider the likelihood of microstatellite instability when evaluating CRCs, particularly those with a Crohn-like response or with >2 TILs per high-powered field.
